text: Estate of Sven Lindqvist, by Karin Lindqvist as Personal Representative, v. Joad Axle Works, No. TC-23-0459, Tamarack County Superior Court. It is a wrongful death action over a June 9, 2022 rollover. The complaint was filed May 30, 2023. Kenge, Carboy & Vholes LLP (Cornelius Vandeleur, partner; Imani Rutherford, associate) represents Joad. Octavia Brandvold represents the Estate.

On June 9, 2022, Sven Lindqvist, 47, was driving a Redfern Freight tractor-trailer down the State Route 114 exit ramp when it rolled onto its side. He died at the scene. The left spindle of the JX-9 tandem drive axle was found separated at the inboard bearing shoulder.

The Estate alleges the spindle fractured first and caused the loss of control. It pleads an inadequate fillet radius and heat treatment, deficient fatigue testing, an economically feasible alternative design, and failure to warn. It claims economic loss above $2.4 million, demands $11.5 million, and seeks punitive damages.

The draft Answer is dated July 14, 2023 and was marked for partner review before filing. The documents do not show whether it was filed. It admits Joad made a JX-9 axle sold in 2018 to a tractor builder and installed in a tractor later operated by Redfern Freight. It denies selling to the decedent or to Redfern directly.

The draft Answer denies any design or manufacturing defect, denies that the spindle separation preceded and caused the loss of control, and says the post-rollover condition of the spindle may result from impact forces.

The draft Answer pleads fifteen defenses. They include state of the art and industry standards, post-sale alteration, inadequate maintenance, superseding cause by third parties (employer, tractor builder, maintenance providers), comparative fault (speed, hours of service, pre-trip inspection), several-only apportionment, adequate warnings, limitations and repose, setoff, no facts supporting punitive damages, preservation of evidence with a joint inspection protocol, and reservation of the right to amend.

The central contested issue is sequence: whether the spindle failed before the rollover (plaintiff's theory) or during it. The memo says that if the separation resulted from the rollover, the design-defect theory collapses.

Plaintiff's metallurgist is Dr. Fenwick Ashdown. He is expected to argue that beach marks show fatigue progression over many months, so the spindle was already cracked before June 9. Plaintiff's reconstructionist is Dr. Lorraine Pettibone. She is expected to say the ramp speed was within the legal limit and that only an axle failure explains the loss of control.

Joad's own metallurgist's preliminary read is that the final overload zone is large and the fracture surface shows heavy smearing from post-separation contact, which is consistent with an impact failure.

Joad's privileged post-accident metallurgical review found a machining tool mark at the fracture origin that the reviewer could not rule out as the initiation point. That report has not been produced and is being withheld as work product. This is a significant adverse risk and should be handled with care in any disclosure or expert-reliance decision.
The tractor's electronic data recorder shows 41 mph on a ramp posted at 35 mph. The firm sees this as supporting comparative fault and an alternative cause.
Fatigue series FT-77, run in 2017, is the center of discovery. Four specimens reached runout and one failed at 82 percent of runout. Plaintiff will argue this shows an inadequate safety margin.

Hollis Pruett, a former Joad test technician who carried out the FT-77 testing and left in 2019, may be deposed by plaintiff on how the testing was conducted. Joad's chief axle engineer, Bertil Oakhurst, ran the 2017 test program and will be a central witness.

Client instruction: Joad will not stipulate to the authenticity of its internal test data, including FT-77, until a protective order is in place. The order must include a tier limiting access to outside counsel and experts. Joad will produce only what the court requires and not before the order is signed. The firm recommends holding the line against any blanket authenticity stipulation, because the data will be a core part of plaintiff's affirmative case.

Plaintiff's counsel asked on October 5, 2023 for a blanket stipulation that Joad's test reports and engineering records are authentic business records. Rutherford declined on October 9. Brandvold then agreed to an attorneys'-eyes-only tier for the test data, and authenticity of specific documents can be discussed once the order is signed.

Protective order status as of mid-October 2023: Rutherford sent a draft with both tiers on October 17. Brandvold said she would sign if the AEO tier covers the FT-77 data and design drawings. Joad also asked that the order bar use of produced material outside this case and require return or destruction at the end. The documents do not show that it was signed.

Agreed discovery scope: Joad will produce JX-9 drawings, the heat-treatment specification, spindle test data including FT-77, and JX-9 spindle warranty and failure reports from 2018 through June 9, 2022. It will also produce JX-9 wheel-end bearing-shoulder reports, which plaintiff requested because the fracture appears to start at the shoulder. Joad refused JX-line-wide reports because the JX-7 and JX-11 have different spindle geometry. Plaintiff will not seek JX-7 or JX-11 data unless discovery shows the JX-9 spindle shares a part with them.

Agreed expert schedule (October 2023 emails): plaintiff's reports March 8, 2024; defense reports June 14, 2024 (about 98 days later); plaintiff's rebuttal July 8, 2024. Joad had first proposed July 8 for defense reports, and plaintiff had first proposed May 6.

Agreed inspection protocols: each side will list the materials its experts considered. Any physical testing of the spindle needs a shared protocol 21 days in advance so both sides can attend. The fractured spindle will not be sectioned without both sides' engineers present. A joint inspection at the storage facility was proposed for the week of November 13, 2023, with the day to be confirmed. The January 2024 memo still lists the inspection protocol and joint lab examination as a February next step.

Joad asked that any deposition of its chief axle engineer take place only after the bearing-shoulder reports have been produced, since his testimony will concern them. The documents do not show plaintiff's answer.
Both sides plan to subpoena Redfern Freight's maintenance records for the tractor, including the last three bearing services. They agreed to share what comes back.

Risks identified in the memo: the FT-77 specimen that failed short of runout; jury sympathy (a widow with two teenage children); the possibility that plaintiff blames Joad's manual if Redfern's last bearing service did not follow the schedule; spoliation; and a punitive claim that alleges no specific facts.
The spindle sat for eight months in a yard before it was moved. The firm must establish chain of custody. The fractured spindle and the tractor are in a storage facility not under Joad's control.

Case assessment (memo of January 22, 2024): this is the most serious exposure in the firm's docket for Joad. The associate estimates a gross verdict range of $3.5 million to $7 million if liability is established, with about a 35 percent probability of an adverse liability finding.

Strategy: the firm's first target should be plaintiff's causation expert. It would test whether the opinion that the spindle was cracked before June 9 rests on testing or replication, whether it rules out separation during the rollover and the 41 mph reading, and what the spindle itself shows. If causation is narrowed, the fillet radius and heat treatment arguments matter far less.

Strategy: develop the industry-standards defense early. Retain Dr. Mathilde Grosvenor, who chairs the relevant standards body's axle subcommittee, to explain what the standards require. She should be engaged separately from Dr. Raul Esquivel, the testifying design engineer who will address this axle's design and testing. Her retention letter should limit her to the standards and their history and keep her work apart from the testing analysis. This avoids one expert vouching for both the design and the yardstick, and shields Dr. Esquivel from cross-examination on committee matters.

Client instruction on experts: the General Counsel wants to review names and credentials of all proposed testifying experts before engagement, wants to know whether anyone will speak to industry practice, and prefers that design testimony stay focused on this axle. He is glad to help identify candidates who have served on standards bodies. The standards-expert plan in the memo should be cleared with him before engagement.

Settlement authority: Joad's insurer, Cobaltridge Indemnity, has pre-approved settlement authority up to $1,500,000. Any offer above that needs written sign-off from Joad's board of directors, and verbal indications from a director or officer are not enough. No offer above $1.5 million should be communicated, even as a signal, without that document. The client needs about three weeks to prepare a board consent. If an offer would fall within the insurer's tier, check with the General Counsel before conveying it.

Settlement recommendation: no settlement talks now, because the sequence evidence is too uncertain and the Estate will price the case on the worst version of the test data. Revisit after the spindle examination. If the sequence picture is favorable, a number in the $1.2 million to $2 million range could be explored. The Estate has made no formal demand beyond the complaint figure.
Anything in the upper half of the $1.2 million to $2 million settlement range would need the board process, which takes about three weeks, so the team must flag it to the client early.

Budget: the client expects $700,000 to $1,000,000 through trial. The memo projects fees and costs of $780,000 to $960,000. Expert and testing costs drive most of the variance. The client wants quotes before any testing is commissioned and wants to know who pays for shared lab work.

Insurance: Joad's policy has a $400,000 retention and an aggregate limit the client is watching closely because of two other open claims. The insurer's claims handler is Perpetua Wallace. She must be copied on anything bearing on coverage and sent the monthly invoice summary. The client wants to hear the same day if the carrier reserves its rights.

Client reporting requirements: a written report every six weeks, with a call after significant events; a first case assessment within 60 days with an exposure range and probability of an adverse result; a phase budget within 45 days; and a short note within five business days after every deposition.

Client standing instructions: route all case communications through the General Counsel, Evander Thorsby. Do not contact current Joad engineers or production staff directly. Make no public statements and refer media, regulator or customer inquiries to him. Limit deposition attendance to one firm lawyer and one insurer lawyer. Give 10 days' notice of any proposed testing. Report immediately any other incidents involving JX-series spindles. Send preservation recommendations, especially for the 2017 test lab. A litigation hold went to Joad's departments on June 15, 2023.

Client instruction on witnesses: interview Bertil Oakhurst early and keep a tight circle around who sees the test files. Neither Oakhurst nor the sales manager for the tractor-builder account (who can discuss how the JX-9 was specified and sold) should be offered for testimony until the firm and the General Counsel have discussed it.

Client view on liability: Joad's engineering department does not believe the JX-9 failed because of its design. The client does not yet know whether the spindle separated before or during the rollover and wants that answered by proper examination before forming a view on liability.
